deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous set of German notes, probably lecture or reading notes on ancient history, about the late Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt. It continues from folio 172 (Physcon's sons) into folio 174 (Alexander II, Auletes, Berenice IV, Cleopatra VII).

Prose content:
- Cleopatra III wanted to put the younger son, Alexander, on the throne. He had to accept the elder son as co-regent.
- The younger received Cyprus and the elder received Egypt.
- In 107 Cleopatra forced Lathyrus to flee and exchange Egypt for Cyprus.
- Lathyrus sought alliances abroad but achieved none.
- Alexander murdered his mother (dated here 89) and had to flee. Lathyrus then returned to the throne and reigned until 81.
- During his reign a revolt broke out at Thebes in Upper Egypt. It held out until 83, when the city was destroyed.
- Lathyrus left a daughter, Berenice, and two sons: Ptolemy Auletes and Ptolemy of Cyprus.

Genealogical tree (death years BC):
- Ptolemy V Epiphanes †181.
  - His sons: Ptolemy VI Philometor †145 and Ptolemy VIII Physcon †117.
    - Physcon's sons: Ptolemy IX Lathyrus †81 (a digit before 81 is struck out) and Ptolemy X Alexander I †88.
      - Lathyrus's children: Berenice (III), Ptolemy XII Auletes and Ptolemy of Cyprus.
      - Alexander I's son: Alexander II.
        - Auletes's children: Berenice (IV), Cleopatra (VII), Arsinoe (IV), Ptolemy (XIII) Dionysus and Ptolemy (XIV) 'Neoteros' (the younger).

Final lines: Alexander II was with the army of Sulla, who was waging war in Asia against Mithridates. This leads into the next page, where Sulla sends him to Egypt to marry Berenice.

No derivations, computations or mathematical problems appear. The handwriting and subject suggest notes taken in a history course; attribution to Gauss himself is uncertain.
errors: Alexander I's murder of his mother Cleopatra III is now dated c. 101 BC, not 89. 89/88 is the date of Alexander's expulsion and Lathyrus's restoration; the note conflates the two events.
The Theban revolt is usually dated 88-85 BC, with Thebes sacked c. 85/84. 'until 83' is slightly off by modern chronology, though plausible for early-19th-century handbooks.
The death years 181 (Epiphanes) and 117 (Physcon) are older conventions; modern dates are 180 and 116 BC. Lathyrus †81 (modern 81/80) and Alexander I †88 are fine.

Auletes and Ptolemy of Cyprus are generally considered illegitimate (or of disputed maternity) sons of Lathyrus. Berenice III was Lathyrus's daughter by Cleopatra Selene, so the tree flattens their status. This is a simplification, not strictly an error.

results.what: Historical notes and genealogical tree of the later Ptolemies (Epiphanes to the children of Auletes)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard ancient-history handbook material (sources: Justin, Pausanias, Porphyry, via 18th/19th-c. compendia)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical (Ptolemaic genealogy and chronology), apparently lecture or reading notes, with no mathematical content. Its presence in the Nachlass is unremarkable.

checkable.asserts: Lathyrus's second reign, from his restoration (89/88 per the note) to his death (81), lasted about 8 years.
Lathyrus's exile in Cyprus, by the note's dates, lasted 18 years.

transcription_corrections: Line 2: 'an[?]nehmen' most likely reads 'anzunehmen' ('den älteren als Mitregenten anzunehmen').
Last name in the tree: 'Neoterus[?]' is Ptolemy (XIV) 'Neoteros' (the younger), written 'Neoterus/Neoteros' and cut off at the margin.
Tree: 'Lathurus +[-X-]81' is correct; a struck-out character precedes 81.
Line 3: the elder brother received 'Aegypten', and the struck-through letters before it ('der ältere Aegypten') are confirmed.
'Alexand. I + 88' and 'Alexand. II' are correct; a vertical stroke links Alexander II beneath Alexander I as his son.
